findings.title: Email comparison is case-sensitive, so blocked emails can be bypassed by changing case
findings.body: Both the `should_block?` lookup (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`) and the model-level `validates :email, uniqueness: true` rely on PostgreSQL's default case-sensitive comparison. An admin who adds `Bad@Spammers.org` to the block list will not block a user signing up with `bad@spammers.org`, because `email = 'bad@spammers.org'` does not match a row stored as `Bad@Spammers.org`. The whole point of the feature is silently defeated for any address whose case differs from the stored row. Normalize on write (e.g. `before_validation { self.email = email.to_s.downcase.strip }`), change the column to `citext` (or add a functional unique index `ON blocked_emails (lower(email))`), and query with `where('lower(email) = ?', value.downcase)`. The same case-folding must be applied to the value passed in from `EmailValidator`.

findings.title: should_block? does a non-atomic read-modify-write and is called twice per request, inflating match_count
findings.body: `should_block?` loads the row, mutates `record.match_count += 1` / `record.last_match_at = ...` in memory, then calls `record.save`. Two issues follow. (1) Lost update under concurrency: two parallel signups for the same blocked email both read `match_count = N`, both set `N+1`, both persist, and the stored value ends at `N+1` instead of `N+2`. Use an atomic update such as `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?, updated_at = ?', Time.zone.now, Time.zone.now)` or `BlockedEmail.increment_counter(:match_count, record.id)`. (2) Double counting within a single request: `UsersController#create` calls `user.valid?` explicitly and then `user.save` (which runs validations again), so `EmailValidator#validate_each` runs twice and `match_count` is incremented twice for every blocked-email attempt, plus twice again for `:do_nothing` matches. Validation callbacks should be pure; if statistics must be tracked, do it in a dedicated counter (e.g. Redis `INCR`) and keep `should_block?` side-effect free.

findings.title: Whitelist/blacklist regex is unanchored, producing false positives
findings.body: `email_in_restriction_setting?` builds the regex as `@(#{domains})` with no start/end anchors. A whitelist entry of `gmail.com` will incorrectly accept (and a blacklist entry will incorrectly reject) addresses like `attacker@gmail.com.evil.com` and `attacker@gmail.comx`, because `String#=~` returns the position of the first substring match. Anchor it as `\A@(#{domains})\z` (or at minimum require a non-word boundary after the captured domain) so the listed domain must run to the end of the address. This bug was carried over from the original `User#email_in_restriction_setting?`, but it now lives in the shared validator and is applied to every model that uses `validates :email, email: true`.

findings.title: EmailValidator spec only covers the blocked-email branch
findings.body: The spec stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and never exercises the whitelist/blacklist branches of `validate_each`, nor the `email_in_restriction_setting?` regex. Because this is the only test for the new validator class, the unanchored-regex bug above (false positives like `attacker@gmail.com.evil.com` against a `gmail.com` whitelist) and any future regressions in whitelist/blacklist handling will not be caught. Add cases that set `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` and `SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist` and assert both false-positive cases and legitimate match/mismatch cases.

findings.title: Unique index on email is case-sensitive, allowing duplicate rows with different case
findings.body: `add_index :blocked_emails, :email, unique: true` uses PostgreSQL's default case-sensitive collation, and the model's `validates :email, uniqueness: true` is also case-sensitive. Together they allow two distinct rows to be inserted for `Bad@Spam.com` and `bad@spam.com`, fragmenting the block list and producing unpredictable `should_block?` results (only the first row in storage order will ever match). Replace the column type with `citext` (enable the extension first) or drop the plain index and add a functional unique index, e.g. `execute "CREATE UNIQUE INDEX index_blocked_emails_on_lower_email ON blocked_emails (lower(email))"`.

findings.title: should_block? swallows save failures and DB exceptions
findings.body: `record.save` is called without checking the return value and without rescuing exceptions. If the update fails (DB connection lost, race with row deletion, future validation error), the function returns based on the in-memory record while no error surfaces to the caller, and any exception raised by `save` will propagate out of `EmailValidator#validate_each` and abort the surrounding `User` validation with an unhelpful `ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid` instead of a clear validation message. At minimum check the return value and log on failure; better, rescue the write so statistics tracking never breaks a real signup.
